title: Food and Wine Pairing in Practice: Designing a Full Menu Pairing
quiz.0.question: What is the basic principle of designing a full menu pairing?
quiz.0.options.0: Open with the most powerful red to show the host's taste
quiz.0.options.1: Use the same wine throughout — easy to manage and no pairing conflicts
quiz.0.options.2: Light to rich, dry to sweet, young to aged — no wine may overshadow the next course
quiz.0.options.3: White with the first course, red with the second, sweet with the third — sweet wine must come last
quiz.0.explanation: The core logic of menu pairing is progression: the palate wakes with light flavours and gradually adapts to more complex ones. If you drink Barolo with the first course, every lighter wine afterwards will seem flat and dull. Going from light to rich ensures each dish is enjoyed at its best.
quiz.1.question: Which Italian wine best suits the "white truffle risotto" at a Piemonte dinner?
quiz.1.options.0: Soave Classico (Veneto, a light, mineral white)
quiz.1.options.1: Amarone della Valpolicella (a rich, powerful red)
quiz.1.options.2: Barbaresco DOCG (Nebbiolo, with earthy, mushroom aromas)
quiz.1.explanation: White truffle risotto is the key dish of a Piemonte dinner. Barbaresco (Nebbiolo) has aged aromas of earth, mushroom and dried leaves that complement white truffle perfectly (both belong to the "earthy" family of flavours). Barbaresco is usually lighter than Barolo and better suited to the risotto before the main course.
quiz.2.question: A guest isn't interested in red wine, but tonight's main course is grilled lamb chops. What is the sommelier's most fitting suggestion?
quiz.2.options.0: Let the guest drink water — pairing must follow the rules
quiz.2.options.1: Recommend a full southern white (such as Fiano di Avellino), whose high acidity and rich body balance the lamb's fat
quiz.2.options.2: Suggest a spirit (grappa) instead, since no red means spirits
quiz.2.options.3: Recommend Moscato d'Asti, whose sweetness neutralises the gaminess of lamb
quiz.2.explanation: The heart of pairing is serving the guest's experience, not enforcing rules. A full southern white (Fiano di Avellino) has enough body, high acidity and minerality to stand up to grilled lamb chops. The sommelier's job is to find a solution the guest enjoys that also suits the food.
quiz.3.question: In menu pairing, what is the key principle for choosing a dessert wine?
quiz.3.options.0: The dessert wine must be less sweet than the dessert, to avoid being cloying
quiz.3.options.1: The dessert wine must be as sweet as or sweeter than the dessert, or the wine will taste sour and bitter
quiz.3.options.2: The dessert wine must be sparkling, as bubbles relieve the heaviness of dessert
quiz.3.options.3: The dessert wine should come from outside Italy for a flavour contrast
quiz.3.explanation: This is the most important structural principle of dessert pairing: the wine must be at least as sweet as the dessert. If the dessert is sweeter than the wine, the wine tastes sour and bitter, completely out of balance. For a rich chocolate cake, for example, choose a Passito or Vin Santo sweeter than Moscato d'Asti.
slides.0.title: Food and Wine Pairing in Practice: Designing a Full Menu Pairing
slides.0.subtitle: Bringing it all together: designing the perfect progression of wines for a five-course Italian menu
slides.1.title: Four Principles of Menu Pairing
slides.1.content:
📈 Principle one: light to rich

Aperitivo → Antipasto → Primo → Secondo → Dolce

The palate wakes up with lighter flavours and gradually adapts to more complex ones; if you drink Barolo with the first course, every lighter wine afterwards will seem flat and dull — the principle you must never break

🍯 Principle two: dry to sweet

Dry → off-dry → sweet (rising sweetness)

Sweet wine almost always comes last; the key rule for dessert wine: the wine must be at least as sweet as the dessert, or it will taste sour and bitter; never pour Moscato d'Asti next to a rich chocolate cake

📅 Principle three: young to aged

Fresh and lively → complex and aged (rising complexity)

Complex aged wines (such as Barolo Riserva) should be saved for the important main course, so guests progress in both taste and understanding; Gavi with the starter and Brunello with the main make a complete journey of flavour

⚖️ Principle four: never overshadow the next

Rising intensity, but no leaps

No wine should be so intense that the next one is eclipsed; if a cheese course follows the main, don't open the richest aged Amarone with the main; leaving room for a final climax is the art of pairing design
slides.2.title: From Aperitif to Main Course: The Pairing Structure in Detail
slides.2.content:
An Italian menu is usually divided into five stages. Each stage has its own pairing logic, and the sommelier must combine them flexibly according to the menu, the occasion and the guests' preferences.

🥂 Aperitivo

Purpose: whet the appetite and open freshly — never cloying or heavy

Wines: Prosecco Brut, Franciacorta Brut, Alta Langa; occasionally a Campari Spritz (made with Prosecco)

🥗 Antipasto

Typical dishes: prosciutto / fresh mozzarella / raw-fish crudo / carpaccio

Wines: light whites (Verdicchio, Pinot Grigio) or light-bodied rosé; fresh acidity that doesn't overpower the ingredients' own sweetness

🍝 Primo Piatto

Typical dishes: pasta / risotto / soup (usually with a sauce that decides the wine)

Wines: medium whites (Greco di Tufo) / light-to-medium reds (Barbera, Chianti); by sauce: tomato → red; cream/seafood → white

🥩 Secondo Piatto

Typical dishes: a large steak / grilled lamb chops / braised pork shank / seafood main

Wines: powerful reds (Barolo, Brunello, Amarone) / full whites (Fiano, for a seafood main); this is the pairing climax of the whole meal
slides.3.title: Cheese and Dessert: The Art of the Finale
slides.3.content:
The last two stages of the menu (cheese + dessert) usually take place in the afterglow of the main-course red, so you must decide whether to change wine and how to finish elegantly.

🧀 The cheese course (Formaggi)

  • Continue the main-course red (if medium in intensity): Chianti Classico can carry on with hard cheese (Pecorino)
  • If there is blue cheese: first serve a dry wine with the other cheeses, then open a sweet wine (Passito/Vin Santo) for the blue cheese last — a dramatic "finale"
  • The versatile choice for a cheese board: Franciacorta Extra Brut or Barbera d'Alba (covering the most cheese types)

🍰 The dessert course (Dolce)

  • Core principle: the wine must be at least as sweet as the dessert, or it will taste sour and bitter
  • Light desserts (panna cotta/fruit tart): Moscato d'Asti (low alcohol 5.5%, delicate floral fruit)
  • Medium desserts (cantucci/baked fruit): Vin Santo or Passito di Pantelleria
  • Rich desserts (chocolate/caramel): aged Vin Santo or Recioto della Valpolicella (a red sweet wine, very sweet)
  • The traditional close: Grappa or Amaro as the final digestif
slides.4.title: A Worked Example: The Full Pairing for an Autumn Dinner in Piemonte
slides.4.content:
The scene: an autumn truffle-season dinner for 6 guests, an important occasion, aiming to showcase local Piemontese character. Here is a complete "regional pairing" proposal.

🥂 Aperitivo

Food: canapés with Piemontese salame and Grana Padano crisps

Wine: Alta Langa DOCG Brut (Piemonte's traditional-method sparkling wine, Pinot Nero + Chardonnay)

Logic: open with a local sparkling wine whose acidity cuts the fat of the salame, showcasing Piemontese identity

🥗 Antipasto

Food: beef tartare, carne cruda all'albese (with shavings of top white truffle)

Wine: Gavi di Gavi DOCG (white Cortese)

Logic: Gavi's fresh minerality doesn't steal the white truffle's show, and its high acidity cleanses the richness of the raw beef

🍝 Primo

Food: white truffle and Fontina risotto, risotto al tartufo bianco e Fontina

Wine: Barbaresco DOCG (Nebbiolo, 5-8 years old)

Logic: Nebbiolo's mushroom and earthy aromas are the most classic complement to white truffle; the creaminess of Fontina is cut by the acidity and tannin

🥩 Secondo & Dolce

Food: Piemontese braised beef, brasato al Barolo (braised in Barolo)

Wine: Barolo DOCG Riserva (10-12 years old)

Logic: a dish braised in Barolo with an aged Barolo — the wine's aromas are already in the dish, creating perfect unity

Dessert: panna cotta → Moscato d'Asti; cantucci → Vin Santo (a tribute to the traditional close)
slides.5.title: Key Takeaways
slides.5.points.0: Four principles of menu pairing: light to rich / dry to sweet / young to aged / no wine overshadows the next
slides.5.points.1: The iron rule of dessert pairing: the wine must be at least as sweet as the dessert, or it tastes sour and bitter
slides.5.points.2: Aperitivo: choose a fresh sparkling wine (Prosecco/Franciacorta) to whet the appetite, avoiding anything cloying
slides.5.points.3: Antipasto: light whites or rosé that don't overpower the ingredients' own sweetness
slides.5.points.4: Primo: decided by the sauce — tomato → light-to-medium red; cream/seafood → white
slides.5.points.5: Secondo: the pairing climax — powerful reds (Barolo/Brunello/Amarone) or full whites (Fiano for seafood)
slides.5.points.6: The cheese course can continue the main-course red; with blue cheese, open a sweet wine (Passito/Vin Santo) last as the finale
slides.5.points.7: A Piemonte dinner example: Alta Langa → Gavi → Barbaresco → Barolo Riserva → Moscato + Vin Santo

slides.6.questions.4.question: At a Piemonte dinner, why does "brasato al Barolo (beef braised in Barolo)" pair best with an aged Barolo?
slides.6.questions.4.options.0: Because a wine from one area must always be paired with food from the same area
slides.6.questions.4.options.1: The dish has absorbed Barolo's aromas during cooking, and an aged Barolo extends and reinforces this flavour link, creating perfect "flavour unity"
slides.6.questions.4.options.2: Because Barolo is the most expensive Italian wine, it is polite to pair it with the most important main course
slides.6.questions.4.options.3: Barolo's tannins disappear completely during braising, so any wine will do
slides.6.questions.4.explanation: Brasato al Barolo braises beef in Barolo, so the whole dish is filled with Nebbiolo's aromas (rose, tar, leather). An aged Barolo directly extends and reinforces this flavour link, letting the dish and the wine form perfect "flavour unity" on the palate — the pinnacle of fine Italian menu pairing.
